analysis.one_liner: Requires every bank to offer a cheap, basic checking-style account for people with low incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after Senator Metzenbaum introduced it in February 1991, it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 1993, with no other senator signing on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every federally insured bank, savings institution, and credit union to offer a basic, low-cost account to people who keep $1,000 or less on deposit. Such accounts could cost no more than the bank's actual cost to run, require no more than $25 to open and $1 to keep open, allow at least 10 withdrawals a month, and let customers use a teller instead of an ATM. Banks would have to post a notice about the account and could be sued by customers for violating the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income people who lack a checking account or find bank fees too high. They would get a guaranteed low-fee account they can use to cash checks, pay bills, and make at least 10 withdrawals a month, without minimum-balance requirements or being forced to bank only by machine.

how_it_helps.text: Every depository institution must offer a basic financial services account with no minimum opening deposit above $25 and no minimum balance above $1 [S3].
The account's maintenance fee, covering all routine service charges, cannot exceed the minimal, reasonable amount the Federal Reserve sets based on the bank's actual processing costs [S3].
Account holders get at least 10 withdrawals per month, monthly statements or a passbook, the right to write checks, and cannot be required to use only ATMs [S3].

Banks cannot condition the account on holding other products or on any prerequisite that discriminates against low-income individuals, and must post a conspicuous notice about the account at every location that takes deposits [S3].

Customers who are denied the account or charged improper fees can recover damages of $100 to $1,000, attorney's fees, and can bring class actions capped at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of the bank's net worth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federally insured banks and other depository institutions, which would have to offer near-cost accounts they currently profit less from, absorb regulatory costs, and face civil liability for non-compliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federally insured banks and credit unions

drawbacks.text: Banks would have to provide near-cost accounts, and the bill does not offset those costs, so small banks and credit unions might bear proportionally larger burdens than large institutions [S3].

The Federal Reserve would have to build a new customer registration program, including an identification card with photograph and signature, adding administrative machinery that could mean delays or paperwork for both banks and customers [S3].
Banks could close an account after 3 overdrafts in 6 months, so customers who frequently overdraw could still lose the account [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: a guaranteed low-fee account for people priced out of banking, backed by real enforcement. The costs fall on banks, which lose fee income on small accounts, and on regulators who must set fee standards and run a registration program. The main design risk is that without cost offsets, banks might recoup losses through fees on other services, but the bill's price controls on the basic account itself are specific and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the bill on February 7, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it stayed without a hearing, a mark-up, or any vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum, an Ohio Democrat, introduced the Basic Banking Services Access Act on February 7, 1991 [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and that referral was the last action of any kind [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Banking Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a hearing, a floor vote, or action in the House before the 102nd Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions are better off, because they never had to offer low-cost accounts to small depositors or face civil liability for refusing, and low-income consumers continue to pay whatever fees the market charges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks, which never had to offer the accounts

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show how the parties would have split; the only record is one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced every federally insured bank, thrift, and credit union to offer near-cost accounts to people with $1,000 or less on deposit, cutting fee income from small accounts and exposing institutions to lawsuits for non-compliance [S3]. Banks' interest in keeping fee structures unchanged ran against low-income customers' need for affordable banking.
By guaranteeing a low-cost transaction account to people with small balances, the bill would have reduced the market for check-cashing outlets and high-fee alternatives to bank accounts [S3].
